Welcome toThe Conical Pendulum

A bob held at an angle, launched sideways — what does the string do?

Listen to the intro

About: the conical pendulum — launch speed, string angle, and angular momentum

Source

Concept
A bob (m = 0.5 kg) on a light string (L = 1 m) launched horizontally from a held angle: what does the string's angle do at different launch speeds, and what happens to the bob's angular momentum about the suspension?
Serves
Investigating whether a conical pendulum can circle steadily at any launch speed, and how the components of its angular momentum about the suspension behave through the motion.
Inquiry
Six sealed prediction cards: rest, gentle, hard, which component survives, the skater consequence, and what the launch sets.
Misconception
"Conserved means it always has the same universal value." The cards probe what a conserved quantity's value actually depends on.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealEvery card commits a choice before the bob is launched; the scene then confirms or refutes it.
Invariant made visibleThe angular-momentum vector sweeps at the suspension while its vertical mark on the axis stands perfectly still.
Earned landmarkThe critical-speed tick on the slider stays hidden until the hunt cards are answered.
Honest integrationThe 3D motion is the sim's own RK4 spherical pendulum; L_z is read from the state, not echoed from a formula.
Target the misconceptionCard 6 makes the half-speed launch give exactly half L_z — conservation fixes whatever the launch created.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Launch at rest

Set the initial angle to 30° and the launch speed to zero. Before releasing the bob, predict the path it follows.

2 · Gentle launch

Keep the angle at 30° and set the launch speed to 1 m s⁻¹. Before launching, predict what the angle of the string does.

3 · Hard launch

Keep the angle at 30° and set the launch speed to 2.5 m s⁻¹. Before launching, predict what the angle does now.

4 · Which part survives

The tension acts along the string and gravity acts straight down. Before running any of the cases again, predict which part of the bob's angular momentum about the suspension point these two forces can never change.

5 · Rate of circling

Return to the 30°, 1 m s⁻¹ launch, in which the string swings inward. Before launching, predict how fast the bob circles the vertical axis as the string comes in.

6 · Half the speed

For the steady launch at 30° the readout shows L_z = 0.42 kg m² s⁻¹. Before launching again at the same angle but at half that speed, predict the value of L_z and what it does afterwards.

The Conical Pendulum

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A bob of mass 0.5 kg hangs from a light string 1 m long. You hold it out at an angle, give it a sideways launch speed, and let go. The sim follows the motion in three dimensions.

What you'll learn

  • How the weight and the string tension together decide the motion of the bob.
  • How the string angle behaves after launches at different speeds.
  • How the angular momentum about the suspension point depends on the launch, and what the two forces do to it.
The apparatus: the held bob (m = 0.5 kg) at angle θ₀ from the vertical axis through O. The ⊙ marks the launch speed v₀, horizontal and out of the page.

What's on screen

  • Bob and string from the pivot ring, with a dashed vertical axis and a labelled θ arc.
  • Launch arrow, shown before and just after release.
  • Path the bob has followed.
  • Force arrows when Forces is ticked: mg, T, and a grey hold before release.
See itLook at the held bob before the release, with the forces on it. Watch for: the bob held at θ = 30°, with arrows for mg, T and the grey hold force.

03

Two forces only: weight and tension

Only two forces act on the bob. The weight mg pulls straight down (4.9 N). The tension T pulls along the string toward the pivot O. Nothing pushes the bob sideways, so any sideways motion comes from the launch alone.

With the launch speed at zero, both forces lie in the vertical plane that contains the string. The bob can never leave that plane. It swings as an ordinary pendulum: down through the lowest point, up to 30° on the other side, and back.

  • One full swing from θ₀ = 30° takes about 2.04 s.
  • The θ readout and the chart show the size of the angle, so they fall from 30° to 0° and rise to 30° again.

A sideways launch adds motion that this plane does not contain, and the path then leaves it.

See itRelease the bob from 30° with no launch speed. Watch for: the bob swinging back and forth in one vertical plane, with θ falling to 0° and rising to 30° again.
04

A steady circle needs one launch speed

For the bob to circle at a constant angle θ, the radius is r = L sinθ and the forces must give no vertical acceleration:

  • Vertical: T cosθ = mg, so T = mg/cosθ.
  • Horizontal: T sinθ = mv²/(L sinθ), the inward force that a circle of radius L sinθ needs.

Dividing the two gives the critical speed vc = √(gL sinθ tanθ). It depends only on the angle. At θ = 30°, vc = 1.68 m/s, T = 5.66 N, the radius is 0.50 m, and one lap takes 2πr/vc = 1.87 s.

Angle θ10°30°60°
vc0.55 m/s1.68 m/s3.83 m/s

Once the sim has revealed it, a vc marker on the launch-speed track shows this speed for the current θ₀.

See itLaunch from 30° at vc = 1.682 m/s. Watch for: the bob circling with θ fixed at 30.0°, and the path a flat ring.
05

Other launch speeds make the angle oscillate

At release the bob moves horizontally, so the angle is momentarily at a turning point. What happens next depends on how v₀ compares with vc.

  • v₀ below vc. At 1 m/s the string pulls the bob inward with 2.37 N, but a circle of radius 0.50 m at that speed needs only 1.00 N. The bob falls inward and θ oscillates between 30° and 17.7°.
  • v₀ above vc. At 2.5 m/s the inward pull is 3.68 N, but the circle needs 6.25 N. The bob drifts outward and θ oscillates between 30° and 45.1°.

The tension does no work on the bob, so only gravity changes its energy, and the motion turns back at both ends. At v₀ = vc the two ends coincide. Each oscillation takes about 1.0 s.

See itLaunch from 30° at 1 m/s, with the angle chart on. Watch for: θ dropping from 30° to about 17.7° and back, again and again.
See itLaunch from 30° at 2.5 m/s. Watch for: θ rising from 30° to about 45.1° and back.
06

The vertical part survives: only Lz is conserved

Take angular momentum about the pivot O. The tension acts along the string, through O, so it has no torque. The weight is vertical, so its torque about O is horizontal and cannot change the vertical component Lz.

So Lz stays fixed through the whole motion, while the other components and the size of the full vector L change whenever θ changes. In the 1 m/s launch, |L| varies between 0.50 and 0.82 kg m²/s.

Lz = m v⊥ L sinθ, where v⊥ is the bob's speed around the vertical axis. At release v⊥ = v₀, so Lz = m v₀ L sinθ₀. For the 1 m/s launch this is 0.250 kg m²/s; for the steady circle at 30° it is 0.420 kg m²/s.

See itLaunch from 30° at 1 m/s and watch the Lz readout while θ swings. Watch for: Lz staying at 0.250 kg m²/s while θ changes between 30° and 17.7°.
07

Circling speeds up as the string comes in

The rate of circling round the axis, φ̇, follows from Lz = mL² sin²θ · φ̇. With Lz fixed, a smaller θ means a larger φ̇, like a skater drawing in the arms.

  • In the 1 m/s launch, φ̇ is 2.00 rad/s at θ = 30° and rises to 5.39 rad/s at 17.7°, a factor of 2.7.

The launch sets Lz, and the motion then keeps it. Half the launch speed at the same angle gives half the Lz: from v₀ = vc = 1.682 m/s to v₀ = 0.841 m/s, Lz falls from 0.420 to 0.210 kg m²/s and stays there. That bob swings in to 14.9° and reaches 6.36 rad/s.

See itLaunch from 30° at 1 m/s, with the angle chart on. Watch for: the bob sweeping round the axis faster each time the string comes in to its smallest angle.
See itLaunch from 30° at 0.841 m/s, half the steady speed. Watch for: Lz reading 0.210 kg m²/s, half of 0.420, and the bob swinging in to about 14.9°.
08

Where it matters

  • Centrifugal governors. For the steady circle, ω² = g/(L cosθ). A faster spin gives a larger θ, so the balls of a Watt governor rise as the engine speeds up.
  • Banked roads. A car on a frictionless bank has a normal force in place of the tension, and the same balance gives v² = rg tanθ.
  • Spinning skaters. Drawing the arms in toward the axis raises the rate of rotation while the angular momentum about the axis stays the same.
Go deeper

The sim has no air drag and no friction at the pivot, so the oscillation of θ never dies away. In a real pendulum, drag would slowly remove Lz. The sim also draws the angle as a size, so a swing past the lowest point shows θ rising again rather than going negative.

09

Summary

In one line. A bob launched sideways from a held angle moves under its weight and the string tension alone, and the sim lets you change the angle and the launch speed.

Key points

  • The steady circle needs vc = √(gL sinθ tanθ), which is 1.68 m/s at 30°.
  • A slower launch makes θ oscillate below θ₀, a faster one above it.
  • Lz = m v₀ L sinθ₀ is set by the launch and never changes afterwards.
  • With Lz fixed, φ̇ = Lz/(mL² sin²θ) rises as θ falls.

Common mix-ups

  • "At a fixed angle the bob always moves in a horizontal circle." Only at vc. At v₀ = 0 it swings in a plane.
  • "Conserved means the same value every time." The launch sets the value. Half the speed gives half the Lz.
  • "The whole angular momentum vector is conserved." Only its vertical component is. |L| changes whenever θ does.

Things to try on your own

  • At θ₀ = 45°, work out vc, enter it, and check that θ stays fixed.
  • At θ₀ = 60° and v₀ = 1 m/s, work out Lz, then compare with the readout.
  • At θ₀ = 30°, compare Lz at 0.5 and 1.0 m/s.
